reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An organic acidaemia caused by deficiency of the biotin-dependent enzyme propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Classic neonatal presentation is life-threatening metabolic decompensation with vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, seizures and severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis
Secondary hyperammonaemia is common and may dominate the picture, and hypoglycaemia and bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) frequently occur

Elevated propionylcarnitine (C3) on acylcarnitine profile with characteristic urine organic acids (e.g. 3-hydroxypropionate, methylcitrate) supports the diagnosis, and MMA is not elevated (distinguishing it from methylmalonic acidemia)
Long-term complications include cardiomyopathy, prolonged QT and arrhythmia, pancreatitis, movement disorder from basal ganglia injury, and developmental delay

Chronic management principles include protein restriction limiting propiogenic amino acids, carnitine supplementation, and control of intercurrent catabolism, with metronidazole sometimes used to lower gut propionate
Unlike some organic acidaemias this disorder is generally not cofactor-responsive, though biotin is often trialled
Included in newborn screening via elevated C3 acylcarnitine, enabling early diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Propionic acidemia arises from deficient propionyl-CoA carboxylase, a mitochondrial biotin-dependent enzyme that converts propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA. This step is part of the catabolic pathway for the amino acids isoleucine, valine, methionine and threonine, as well as odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol. Enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of propionyl-CoA and its derivatives (propionic acid, 3-hydroxypropionate, methylcitrate, propionylcarnitine). These organic acids produce severe metabolic acidosis, inhibit the urea cycle to cause hyperammonaemia, impair mitochondrial energy production, and are toxic to the myocardium, bone marrow, pancreas and basal ganglia.
additionalDifferentials: Isovaleric acidemia and other organic acidaemias
additionalInvestigations: Blood gas with anion gap, glucose, lactate and ammonia
Urine organic acids (methylcitrate, 3-hydroxypropionate) and plasma acylcarnitine (elevated C3)
Cardiac evaluation with ECG and echocardiography for cardiomyopathy and QT prolongation
redFlags: Acute metabolic decompensation with severe acidosis and hyperammonaemia is a medical emergency
Cardiomyopathy or QT prolongation with risk of life-threatening arrhythmia
Rapid clinical deterioration during infection, fasting or catabolic stress
reference.prognosis: Propionic acidemia is among the more severe organic acidaemias, with high risk of recurrent metabolic crises and long-term neurological and cardiac complications despite treatment; early detection and rigorous metabolic management improve survival, and selected patients are considered for liver transplantation.
pitfalls: Confusing it with methylmalonic acidemia without checking that methylmalonic acid is not elevated
Overlooking cardiac surveillance, since cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia can be fatal even with good metabolic control
Attributing the acidotic neonate to sepsis and delaying specific therapy
Under-recognising secondary hyperammonaemia as a driver of encephalopathy
management: Institute lifelong dietary protein restriction limiting the propiogenic amino acids isoleucine, valine, methionine and threonine, using specialised propiogenic-free medical formula under dietetic supervision
Supplement L-carnitine to replenish carnitine and promote excretion of propionyl esters, and give intermittent metronidazole to reduce gut bacterial propionate production
Provide an emergency regimen for intercurrent illness with cessation of natural protein and high-energy glucose intake to suppress catabolism, avoiding prolonged fasting

Manage acute decompensation with intravenous dextrose and insulin to reverse catabolism, ammonia-scavenging agents for hyperammonaemia, and haemofiltration or dialysis for severe hyperammonaemia or acidosis
Undertake surveillance for known complications including cardiomyopathy and QT prolongation with ECG and echocardiography, pancreatitis, cytopenias and neurodevelopmental delay
Consider liver transplantation in selected patients with recurrent crises or poor metabolic control
Manage through a metabolic multidisciplinary team and provide genetic counselling with family and newborn screening, given autosomal recessive inheritance
